questions.title: Sutures help wound healing by apposing edges
questions.question: A 20-year-old woman sustains an injury to her right calf in a mountain biking accident. On physical examination she has a 5 cm long laceration on the right lateral aspect of her lower leg. This wound is closed with sutures. Wound healing proceeds over the next week. Which of the following factors will be most likely to help wound healing in this patient?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Corticosteroid therapy impairs, not helps, healing -- it suppresses the inflammatory and fibroblastic phases of repair.
explanations.B: Correct. The presence of sutures apposes the wound edges, minimising the gap the repair process must bridge. This favours quicker, first-intention-style healing with less granulation tissue. It is the one factor here that helps rather than impairs the wound's outcome.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Decreased tissue perfusion impairs healing by limiting the oxygen and nutrient delivery the repair process depends on.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The presence of bacteria impairs healing by prolonging the inflammatory phase and directly damaging newly formed tissue.

questions.topic: Tissue repair: Factors affecting and complications
questions.learning_objective: Identify apposing sutured wound edges as a factor that helps healing, distinct from corticosteroid therapy, decreased perfusion and bacterial contamination, which all impair it.

questions.title: A surgical wound does not heal by second intention
questions.question: The following lesion does NOT heal by second intention:

explanations.A: Correct. A surgical wound is typically a clean, incised defect whose edges can be closely apposed, for example with sutures. This lets it heal by first intention -- primary union with minimal granulation tissue -- rather than by second intention. It is therefore the standard example of a lesion excluded from the second-intention pathway.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the answer. An abscess cavity is a defect that cannot be apposed and heals by second intention, filling with granulation tissue.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the answer. An area of ulceration is a tissue-loss defect that heals by second intention, not by primary apposition.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the answer. An infarct undergoing repair heals through organisation and, where there is a resulting tissue defect, by second-intention-style granulation and scarring, not by apposed-edge primary union.

questions.title: Second intention healing has more common complications
questions.question: Which of the following is a feature of healing by second intention?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A clean wound with apposed edges is the setting for first, not second, intention healing.
explanations.B: Correct. Healing by second intention fills a larger tissue defect with abundant granulation tissue. It heals by wound contraction over a longer time than first intention. Because of this larger defect and longer course, it carries a higher rate of complications.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Second intention healing specifically follows a larger, not minimal, tissue loss -- that is why it needs abundant granulation tissue to fill the gap.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Second intention healing carries a higher, not a nil, infection risk, given the larger open defect and longer healing time.

questions.topic: Tissue repair: Factors affecting and complications
questions.learning_objective: State that more common complications, not clean wounds, minimal tissue loss or no infection, is the feature of healing by second intention.

questions.title: First intention healing occurs in a clean cut wound
questions.question: Which of the following is characteristic for healing by first intention?

explanations.A: Correct. First intention healing occurs in a clean, incised wound whose edges are closely apposed. It needs only a thin fibrin seal and minimal granulation tissue to close the gap. This is why it heals faster and with fewer complications than second intention.
explanations.B: Incorrect. More common complications is a feature of second, not first, intention healing.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Abundant granulation tissue is needed to fill the larger defect of second intention healing, not the minimal gap of first intention.
explanations.D: Incorrect. First intention healing is comparatively quick, not slow -- taking a long time to heal is instead characteristic of second intention.

questions.learning_objective: State that occurring in a clean cut wound, not more complications, abundant granulation tissue or a long healing time, is characteristic of first intention healing.
